title: The mobile visit for an education product
metaTitle: Education product mobile website first screen
excerpt: The first phone screen has to show the lesson and a way to start a class or a trial. Design that screen first. Do not shrink the desktop.
alt: A wide mountain valley with snowy peaks, a braided river, and evergreen trees in the foreground, a long view the phone still has to crop to one path.

faqs.question: What is on the first phone screen?
faqs.answer: The learning-moment sentence, one readable frame of the product, and the right start: a class or a trial. If both audiences share the URL, stack two labeled starts. Do not hide the choice inside a single button called Get started.

faqs.question: How do you know the desktop was allowed to decide?
faqs.answer: The phone page is a shrunk dashboard, type that needs a pinch, or captions that only appear on hover. Hover does not exist on a phone. Rebuild the narrow screen, then add width only where the lesson stays legible.

faqs.question: What speed should you aim for?
faqs.answer: Use Google's Core Web Vitals targets. Largest contentful paint should land within 2.5 seconds, the page should respond to input within 200 milliseconds, and layout shift should stay under 0.1. Serve a phone-sized image of the lesson, and skip a cinematic hero that hides the exercise.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
Most teachers and parents will judge an education product mobile website before they ever see the desktop. The first screen still has to show the learning moment and a way to start a class or a trial. Do not let the desktop composition decide the phone page.

A wide dashboard, shrunk until the badges are texture and the button sits under a fold, is not a mobile visit. It is a slide that survived. This buyer is between classes or in a pickup line. They will not turn the phone sideways to rescue your layout.

## The phone is the real first visit

A teacher gets a link from another teacher and opens it with one minute on the clock. A parent gets a link in a message and opens it with a child nearby, or after the child is asleep and the decision has to be quick. Neither visit looks like a design review on a monitor. Design the first look for that glass.

[Nielsen Norman Group's research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) gives you the budget. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds unless the value is clear in about 10, and they read only about a quarter of the text. On a phone the screen holds less of that quarter. The value is the learning moment plus the start. If a badge chart or a mission statement occupies the first viewport, you have spent the budget on the team.

Treat the phone as the original. Write the sentence so it wraps in two or three lines at a narrow measure. Crop the product so the exercise is readable in that width. Add a side-by-side classroom scene only when the screen is wide enough to keep the lesson legible. Teams that start on a desktop protect the desktop. They stack leftover columns and call it responsive. The phone then looks like an apology for a slide.

Do the test on a phone you did not design on, in a hallway or outside. Ask someone who has not seen the desktop what the learner does and how they would start. If they say "an app for schools" and cannot describe the activity, the first screen failed. Do not go back upstairs to admire the wide version. Change the narrow one.

## What the first screen holds

Four things, and nothing that pushes them away. The sentence of the learning moment. One readable frame of the practice or the teacher view. The action, Start a class or Start a trial, in the words that match the reader you are addressing. A line that says who it is for, if the sentence did not already. A logo may sit in the bar. A second slogan may not. A newsletter may not. A cookie wall that hides the lesson may not, if you can avoid it.

If teachers and parents share this URL, the first screen can show the moment once and offer two labeled starts, stacked, with enough space to tap. Do not hide the choice in a single Get started button that branches after they have already committed their email. Routing belongs where they can see it.

The product frame has to be re-cropped for the width, not squeezed. A three-column teacher dashboard becomes a blur. Show the one column that is the decision, usually the list of who is stuck or the single exercise. Put the rest one scroll away, or cut it from the marketing page entirely. You are not demoing every panel. You are proving there is a lesson.

The button has to be thumb-reachable and visible without a sticky bar that covers the exercise. Place it in the flow under the frame, and repeat it after the next proof. One path, twice. Not a sticky bar plus a chat bubble plus an app-store badge. Those are three exits, and two of them skip the lesson.

## Do not inherit the desktop

Type that was huge on a projector-sized layout becomes a poster on a phone, and the lesson starts off screen. Type that was merely scaled down becomes too small to read, and the parent pinches. Set sizes by reading them on a device. Comfortable line length. Space between the sentence, the frame, and the action so they are three ideas, not a clump.

Hover is not a mobile event. Captions that appear only on hover do not exist for this buyer. Put the caption under the picture. Tooltips that explain the badge do not exist either, which is another reason not to lead with badges. If a comparison needed a slider, use two labeled images stacked. Sliders are easy to miss and easier to break with a thumb.

The menu should list the same jobs as the wide bar. For teachers, for families, pricing, the start, log in in a quieter spot. Do not invent a phone-only set of links. [The W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the floor: text has to be perceivable, controls have to be operable. A thin, pale menu fails outdoors, which is where pickup lines are. Large type. Obvious targets. The word Start a trial spelled out.

Motion should be quieter here, not cleverer. A parallax classroom that stutters will be closed. If anything moves, it should be a short change of state, and reduced motion should show the same lesson immediately. Do not autoplay a film of children. Apart from the performance and the consent problem, the film steals the ten seconds from the exercise.

## What to keep and what to cut

Keep the learning-moment sentence, the readable product frame, the right start button, and the name of the product. Keep one line of boundary if it prevents a false hope, such as "one skill, ten minutes, you do not have to teach it." Keep a way to pricing and to the other audience.

Cut the badge dashboard. Cut the logo wall of schools. Cut the three-column philosophy. Cut side-scrolling marquee text. Cut any image that existed to balance a desktop composition. Cut a video hero. On a phone, extra ornaments become walls between a tired adult and the start.

Rewrite, do not only reflow. A caption that sat beside a wide image may need to move above it so they know what the crop is. A pricing table may need to become stacked offers with the trial details visible. A long founder letter should not appear at all. If the only note to engineering is "make it work on mobile," the design is not done.

Use real copy in the test. The longest skill name. The longest button, Start a class. A trial sentence that includes "no card" or "card at the end," whichever is true. Optimistic sample words hide overflow until a parent sees a broken button and decides the product will be broken too.

Ask almost nothing in the first screen's form, if you ask anything. Often the button should go to a short start page rather than expand a form over the lesson. Ten fields on a phone will cost you the class you just explained. The contact or signup path can ask for the grade and the role. It should still ask for little.

## Speed on a shared phone

The learning moment is not there if the image has not arrived. Google's Core Web Vitals are the practical bar for the page they actually load: largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, interaction to next paint within 200 milliseconds, and layout shift under 0.1. Those thresholds are in [Google's Core Web Vitals documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals). A parent on a school-night connection and a teacher on a cart of aging laptops are the users to picture, not the newest phone in the studio.

Serve a phone-sized image of the lesson, with width and height reserved so the button does not jump down when the picture lands. Do not load a desktop screenshot and a background video and a font that delays the sentence. The sentence should be readable even before the image, in HTML, not trapped inside a picture of a headline.

A plain page with one sharp crop will feel more serious than a cinematic page that spins. Hanabi builds this kind of marketing site to be fast before it is clever, with Next.js on Vercel and images that have a size and a job. You can use another stack. You cannot skip the refusal. A hero that costs the first ten seconds has hidden the lesson.

Test on a middling phone. If it is smooth only on yours, it is not smooth for the classroom.

## A review between bells

Set a timer. Open the homepage. At ten seconds, say what the learner does and which button you would press. If you mention badges, mission, or the company story, the first screen is wrong. Replace it. Do not add a section under it and hope they scroll. Many will not.

Then start the action. The next page should load quickly and tell a teacher or a parent what happens next, what to have ready, and how fast a person replies if a person is part of the path. If the button opens a form with ten fields, you wasted the hallway test.

Do this on the live site after launch. Staging images are often lighter. Ask one teacher or one parent, not a teammate, to try the same ten seconds. Believe them if they cannot find the lesson.

That next page is its own design. [A contact path for an education product](/blog/a-contact-path-for-an-education-product) should say what happens after they reach out, how fast, and what to have ready. The action is still to start a class or a trial. A long form is how you lose the person the phone page just convinced.

When you want a reference for a first screen that survives a narrow column, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) and do the hallway test on your current site before the call. Bring what you could say at ten seconds. The useful work is a shorter first screen, not a more impressive desktop.
